title: Canvassing

jokes.text: Tom hides the eggs, and I have to say he did an exceptional job this year. I've been searching for 25 minutes and I haven't found a single egg. And I'm an adult.
jokes.setup: Leslie praises Tom's egg-hiding as 'exceptional' — sounds like a compliment about his effort.
jokes.punchline: The 'exceptional job' means no eggs have been found at all. The added detail 'And I'm an adult' lands the absurdity of the failure.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection opener. The praise sets up an expectation that is immediately undercut. 'And I'm an adult' is the kicker that elevates it from a simple reversal to a character beat — Leslie's earnest self-awareness makes it funnier. Good economy, well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, this is incredible. You've hidden these eggs so well that I, an adult woman with a fully developed prefrontal cortex, cannot find a single one.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, about that... I forgot to hide them.

jokes.text: Oh. Yeah, I forgot to do that.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been earnestly defending Tom's egg-hiding effort as a deliberate challenge while searching for 25 minutes.
jokes.punchline: Tom casually admits he simply forgot to hide any eggs at all, demolishing Leslie's charitable interpretation.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is delivered with maximum economy — five words that collapse the entire setup. Tom's breezy indifference is perfectly in character. The rewatch bonus is strong because the first viewing makes you believe the premise; on rewatch the pause before his admission is funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My mother is like Margaret Thatcher, but beautiful.

jokes.text: Maybe Tom's trying to make this year a challenge. And if so, he's succeeding. I don't think a single egg has been found yet. Let's keep looking. We're gonna find one.
jokes.setup: Tom has just admitted he forgot to hide the eggs.
jokes.punchline: Leslie continues to spin the disaster positively, doubling down on her optimistic interpretation rather than accepting reality.
jokes.explanation: This is Leslie's defining character trait — relentless, reality-defying optimism — introduced in the very first scene. The joke works because it escalates the delusion: even after the admission, she keeps going. High character integration because this moment seeds her entire arc. Slightly bloated in execution.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I wasn't really inviting you anyway. I just wanted to see if you'd make an excuse.

dialogue.speaker: Myrtle
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I knew you were going to say no, so I preemptively rejected you so I could reject you first.

jokes.text: She's as respected as Mother Teresa. She's as powerful as Stalin, and she's as beautiful as Margaret Thatcher.
jokes.setup: Leslie builds up her mother with two flattering comparisons — Mother Teresa and Stalin (powerful).
jokes.punchline: The final comparison, 'as beautiful as Margaret Thatcher,' subverts the pattern. Thatcher is not conventionally cited for beauty, making it a backhanded compliment Leslie is completely oblivious to.
jokes.explanation: Strong rule-of-three structure. The Stalin inclusion is already funny (powerful ≠ complimentary), but the Thatcher punchline lands harder because Leslie means it sincerely. The joke reveals her obliviousness and her complicated relationship with her mother simultaneously. High quotability because it's a complete, self-contained unit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When I was in third grade, I ran for student council president. I got more votes than voters existed.

jokes.text: In or out, Leslie. Doorway is creepy.
jokes.setup: Leslie is hovering in the doorway of her mother's office, unsure whether to enter.
jokes.punchline: Her mother's blunt, oddly specific observation — 'Doorway is creepy' — immediately establishes the power dynamic and the mom's no-nonsense personality.
jokes.explanation: Three words that do real work: they're funny, they characterize the mom, and they reframe Leslie's nervous hovering as a social infraction. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everyone needs to put sunscreen on their beaks!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm good. I don't need sunscreen.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, everyone needs sunscreen.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Not me. I'm black.

jokes.text: Oh. That's weird. I just remembered something. I have my own subcommittee now.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been fumbling through excuses to leave her mom's office without sharing her real news.
jokes.punchline: She pretends to 'just remember' the subcommittee — obviously the whole reason she came — as if it's a casual afterthought.
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's transparently fake spontaneity. The audience (and mom) can see through it immediately, but Leslie commits fully. Good character moment showing her neediness for approval.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't handle the pit! Son, we live in a world that has pits, and those pits have to be filled by men with shovels. Who's gonna do it? You? You, Lieutenant Weinstein? I have a greater responsibility than you could possibly fathom. You weep for the hole and you curse the Parks Department. You have that luxury. You have the luxury of not knowing what I know — that the pit's destruction, while tragic, probably saved lives. And my existence, while grotesque and incomprehensible to you, saves pits!

jokes.text: Leslie tells her mom about the subcommittee: 'Yeah. I'm sure you've heard something about it. People are talking about it.' Her mom: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confidently asserts that her subcommittee is the talk of the town
jokes.punchline: Her mom flatly says 'No' — one syllable destroying Leslie's entire premise
jokes.explanation: The single-syllable devastation is perfectly timed and character-appropriate. Leslie's rising excitement versus mom's complete indifference is a running dynamic well-served here. The economy of 'No' is nearly perfect for this beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And another thing, the parks department really cares about community engagement, so if you just give us a chance—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hello? Where did you go?

jokes.text: You want to come? / Oh. Honey, jeez. You know how busy I am. / I know. I know. I know! That's why I fake invited you.
jokes.setup: Leslie invites her mom to the town hall, the mom gives a non-committal brush-off, and Leslie starts agreeing with her excuses.
jokes.punchline: 'That's why I fake invited you' — Leslie admits preemptive self-protection while immediately undercutting her own coolness by still wanting her mom to come.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'I fake invited you' is a perfectly coined phrase that most people recognize from real life but have never heard named so precisely. It's character-specific (only someone as approval-hungry as Leslie would self-protect this way), structurally tight, economical, and quotable. The follow-up 'I'll try to be there' hitting right after confirms her mom understood the real invitation all along, adding a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: Do you have a playground? My kids love playgrounds! And a splash pad would be amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, we're actually planning to expand both of those amenities. How many children do you have?

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: Oh, none. I just like to use the equipment.

jokes.text: The metal folding chair bang during the meeting setup — 'Ow! Sorry. Oh, I'm sorry. Metal. Sorry. That's really loud.'
jokes.setup: Leslie calls the subcommittee to order with an air of authority.
jokes.punchline: Someone bangs a metal folding chair, creating a jarring noise that completely deflates the moment.
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy that undercuts Leslie's authority. The rapid apologies are a nice rhythm, but the joke is fairly generic and could happen in any workplace comedy. Low character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: How far is the park from schools?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Um, about two blocks. Why do you ask?

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: And how far from a library? A community center? A playground?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm... not sure where you're going with this.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: I just need to know the distance from my house to the park.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that depends on your address.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: Right, so I'm going to need a map with a 500-yard radius drawn around my residence.

jokes.text: When I was in sixth grade, I was voted Best Dressed by 87 votes. And there were only 63 people in my class.
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a case for canvassing by citing her expertise at changing hearts and minds.
jokes.punchline: Her proof of persuasion skills is winning a vote with more votes than voters — which implies fraud, not persuasion, though Leslie seems unaware of the implication.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. It operates on multiple levels simultaneously: it's absurd (impossible math), it's character-specific (Leslie's total lack of self-awareness about what this implies), it has perfect economy, and it foreshadows her political ambitions while subtly suggesting she's always been ethically flexible in pursuit of her goals without knowing it. The math lands like a punchline after the beat of realization. Highly quotable, genuinely original construction.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He runs like a newborn baby giraffe.

jokes.text: How many more Pawnee citizens are gonna have to fall into that pit before we turn it into a park? Zero. Say it. Zero. A hundred. Zero.
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to get Ann to commit to the inspiring answer 'zero' in a call-and-response.
jokes.punchline: Ann responds 'A hundred' — either misunderstanding the game or deliberately being difficult — forcing Leslie to repeat the prompt.
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of the exchange is well-constructed. 'A hundred' as the wrong answer is perfectly timed and lands hard because it's so specifically wrong — not just a shrug, but a confident wrong number.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, why don't you just have the 4-year-old babysit the 2-year-old?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: What? No, that doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why not? The 4-year-old is twice as old as the 2-year-old. That's perfect.

jokes.text: I've got some sunscreen for your beaks. Tom, you probably won't need any.
jokes.setup: Leslie is distributing sunscreen to the canvassing team.
jokes.punchline: The aside to Tom — 'you probably won't need any' — is a reference to his darker complexion, delivered with complete innocence by Leslie.
jokes.explanation: Classic early Parks cringe — Leslie's well-meaning obliviousness around race. The humor comes entirely from her cluelessness rather than malice. 'Beaks' is also a slightly odd word choice that adds texture. Moderately effective cringe comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mickey, listen. I'm gonna be straight with you. You seem like a smart guy, a guy who makes good decisions. So I'm gonna need you to commit to this deal right now. Because if you don't... you're a bitch.

jokes.text: The canvassing guide with branching paths — 'If a person is a man, turn to page two.' / 'If the person looks like a celebrity, example, Jack Nicholson, use this to help your pitch. Example: You can't handle the pit. That's why we need to turn it into a park.'
jokes.setup: Leslie presents what she calls a canvassing guide — suggesting it will be a simple script.
jokes.punchline: The guide is a branching Choose-Your-Own-Adventure document, including a section for if the citizen looks like Jack Nicholson, with a A Few Good Men pun that is simultaneously groan-worthy and actually kind of clever.
jokes.explanation: The absurdist specificity is the joke: not just 'here's a script,' but a whole decision tree with celebrity contingency plans. The 'You can't handle the pit' line is a pun that works better than it should because of how committed Leslie is to it. Strong character integration — this level of over-preparation is quintessentially Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We need to cool down. I'm going to go bury myself in the woods.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine. I'll bury you instead.

jokes.text: Leslie divides the team into Even and Odd sectors, declares 'We're gonna win!' and Mark asks flatly: 'Win what?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has pumped up the team with military-style sector assignments and a rallying cry
jokes.punchline: Mark asks 'Win what?' — deflating the competitive framing since this is just a park proposal, not a competition
jokes.explanation: Two words, complete joke. 'Win what?' is a perfect deadpan deflation of Leslie's excessive competitive framing. Mark's voice as skeptical realist is well-used here. Maximum economy — the joke is entirely in those two words and the pause they create.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, did you actually conduct this survey about nuclear waste storage?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I mean... not exactly. I may have just made up all the data.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You made it up? The entire survey?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, the results I needed were obvious. People don't want nuclear waste. I just saved us six months of paperwork.

jokes.text: Are you excited? Excited, yeah. Are you ready? Yes, definitely. Are you pumped up? Yes! Look humble. But confident.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann approach their first door, and Leslie runs through a rapid pep-talk checklist.
jokes.punchline: 'Look humble. But confident.' — the contradiction is the joke, and the deadpan delivery sells it as if it's actionable advice.
jokes.explanation: The escalating pep talk is slightly standard, but 'Look humble. But confident.' is a well-earned punchline. The contradiction delivered as sincere coaching is very Leslie and lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, we did a survey. We surveyed meth users about their favorite parks.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: You surveyed meth users?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. Very helpful focus group, actually. Super engaged. Lots of energy.

jokes.text: How would you feel if we turned that pit into a beautiful community park? / Oh. Yeah. That'd be a great idea. / Oh. Good. / I actually live in the neighborhood so I could probably tell you a little bit about... / That's... Go to section three.
jokes.setup: Their first canvassing interaction goes well — the neighbor is enthusiastic and starts to volunteer local knowledge.
jokes.punchline: Leslie ignores the genuinely helpful input and robotically follows the script, cutting the neighbor off to go to 'section three.'
jokes.explanation: The joke pays off the absurd canvassing guide: Leslie is so committed to her system that she overrides a cooperative citizen to stay on script. Good callback that reveals character (she needs control) while also being observationally funny about bureaucratic over-preparation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You don't even care about your own children! If you did, you would support this park initiative because it's good for families and the community!

jokes.text: Now, is this park gonna have a playground or, you know, maybe a pool for the kids? / Oh, how old are your kids? / No kids.
jokes.setup: A male neighbor asks enthusiastically about amenities for his kids.
jokes.punchline: He has no kids. The question was entirely for himself.
jokes.explanation: Efficient setup/punchline with a well-timed beat. The subtext (lonely adult man who wants a playground) is a little dark, which makes it funnier. The 'Uh-oh' reaction implied from Leslie and Ann adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Angry Parent
dialogue.line: When is the meeting?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, it's actually pretty boring. You probably don't want to come. It's just a lot of... bureaucratic stuff. Very dry. Very technical.

dialogue.speaker: Angry Parent
dialogue.line: What time?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: 7 PM. Town Hall. Conference Room B. Bring a pen.

jokes.text: Also, is the park gonna be at least 1,000 feet from my house? Because, you know, I really can't move again.
jokes.setup: The neighbor has been asking normal questions about the park.
jokes.punchline: The 1,000-foot question is a sex offender registry requirement, and 'I really can't move again' implies he's had to before.
jokes.explanation: Dark and unexpected. The 1,000-foot reference is well-known enough that the implication lands immediately, and 'I really can't move again' is a beautifully understated escalation. Gets a big surprised laugh. The joke is economical and the darkness comes from implication rather than statement.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey ladies, are you landscapers? Because I'd like to get up in those thighs and do some serious mulching.

jokes.text: April, please stand behind me. / That's it. That's all. That's all we've got. No flier? / Nope.
jokes.setup: After the neighbor's disturbing revelation, Leslie tries to wrap up the interaction.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's only damage-control move is to physically position April behind her, and the 'No flier? Nope.' exchange reveals they have absolutely nothing to leave him with.
jokes.explanation: Quick button on the disturbing neighbor scene. The protective instinct for April is a nice character moment for Leslie. The 'no flier' exchange reveals the operation's underprepared reality despite all the guide complexity. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need an injured candidate. Someone sympathetic. Someone in a wheelchair.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy! We'll put Andy in a wheelchair.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's perfect. FDR was in a wheelchair and he was the greatest president ever.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie, FDR hid his wheelchair from the American people.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly. But we'll do the opposite. We'll flaunt it.

jokes.text: Wow, man. This is great. This is so great. I love canvassing. What a great way to spend my time. All right, Team Haverford. You guys are awesome, but I think I might work better as a solo artist. So, I'm gonna head out. Peace.
jokes.setup: Tom has been feigning enthusiasm for canvassing.
jokes.punchline: His over-the-top performance of loving it transitions immediately into ditching the team, calling himself a 'solo artist' — the language of a performer, not a civil servant.
jokes.explanation: 'Solo artist' is doing a lot of work here — it's Tom's self-image as a cool creative person colliding with the reality of canvassing for a city park. High character integration; this is Tom in miniature. Slightly overlong setup before the pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The government has no business spending taxpayer money on programs. It's wasteful, inefficient, and fundamentally un-American.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Wait, you're telling me they actually... they actually implemented these programs? They're building things? Creating jobs?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: This is a nightmare. This is the exact opposite of what I stand for.

jokes.text: He runs weird. He really does.
jokes.setup: Tom has just dramatically declared himself a solo artist and left.
jokes.punchline: Leslie and Ann watch him run away and share a simple, honest observation about his running style.
jokes.explanation: A small visual gag dependent on the performance. Works as a deflating coda to Tom's grand exit. 'He really does' from Ann adds a conspiratorial warmth between the two women. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: In Russia, they don't have parks like we do. They have these empty fields where old men sit on rocks and pretend they're potatoes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That sounds efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not efficient, Ron, it's sad.

jokes.text: Okay. Which part are you not sure about? / Turning the pit into a park. / That's kind of the whole thing.
jokes.setup: A neighbor says he's 'not sure' about the proposal.
jokes.punchline: His uncertainty is about the entire concept — not a detail but the fundamental premise — which Leslie calls out with exasperated precision.
jokes.explanation: 'That's kind of the whole thing' is a clean, well-timed line. It captures Leslie's mounting frustration while staying funny rather than shrill. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: First we'd visit the park, and then we'd go to the White House, and then... well, one thing leads to another, and suddenly I'm the first female President of the United States.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's exactly how it works.

jokes.text: Could the 4-year-old watch the 2-year-old?
jokes.setup: A neighbor says she'd love to come to the forum but can't get a babysitter for her young kids.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, with complete sincerity, suggests the 4-year-old could supervise the 2-year-old.
jokes.explanation: Short, sharp, and perfectly in character. Leslie is so focused on getting this citizen to the meeting that she's willing to suggest genuinely dangerous childcare. The deadpan delivery is essential — she's not joking. One of the episode's most economical jokes and a great character reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to postpone the town meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: On what grounds?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm thinking... somewhere between now and the heat death of the universe.

jokes.text: Are you gonna commit to coming to this meeting tomorrow, or are you gonna be a bitch?
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to pressure a contractor into attending the meeting.
jokes.punchline: His 'persuasion' technique escalates to calling the contractor a bitch as a closing argument — framed as a binary choice between commitment and cowardice.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of the tonal whiplash — Tom has been smooth-talking, and suddenly deploys a blunt insult as if it's a standard negotiating tactic. Very Tom Haverford: confident, inappropriate, somehow effective.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Don, I've created the perfect jingle for your cement company. Ready? *clears throat* 'Don's Cement, it's really hard, keeps your driveway looking—'

dialogue.speaker: Don
dialogue.line: That doesn't rhyme.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It will when people sing it faster.

jokes.text: Nose to the grindstone. No means yes.
jokes.setup: Tom is recapping his canvassing philosophy.
jokes.punchline: 'No means yes' as a motivational canvassing mantra is both a dark joke and a perfect Tom worldview encapsulation.
jokes.explanation: Three words that land as both a character joke and a subtle commentary on Tom's approach to life. The 'earned vs. cheap' score is slightly lower because the dark implication of 'no means yes' is probably unintentional in context.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I really need you to support the park if I'm called on. This is important.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Probably.

jokes.text: Can we stop, please? Because it's really hot, and I'm tired. / Yeah, I'm hot, too. Let's blow on each other's faces.
jokes.setup: Ann asks to take a break from canvassing because of the heat.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate solution is for them to blow on each other's faces — a completely impractical, childlike response that she suggests with total earnestness.
jokes.explanation: 'Let's blow on each other's faces' is a great absurdist image — simultaneously intimate, impractical, and delivered with complete sincerity. It's the kind of thing a determined but somewhat oblivious person would actually suggest. Good character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: This is going to be a disaster. I can feel it in my bones. Someone's going to say something stupid, someone's going to get angry, and by the end of it, we'll all be wishing we called in sick.

jokes.text: This is a little something I learned from Karl Rove. If you want to guarantee the results of a survey, you design the question to give you the answer that you want. 'Wouldn't you rather have a park than a storage facility for nuclear waste?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has a sealed 'secret weapon' envelope for Ann.
jokes.punchline: Her Karl Rove-inspired strategy is a push poll with a cartoonishly unfair alternative ('nuclear waste storage facility') — she's simultaneously mocking political manipulation and using it without irony.
jokes.explanation: The Karl Rove namedrop works because it's politically specific without being preachy. The nuclear waste example is the right degree of absurd — clearly unfair but not so outlandish it's pure absurdism. Leslie's sincere deployment of the trick she's describing is the real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They're real people! They exist! I have their names written down!

jokes.text: That seems iffy. / Yeah, don't worry about it, I made it all up.
jokes.setup: Ann expresses mild concern about the push poll's honesty.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'I made it all up' is delivered as a complete reassurance rather than an admission of wrongdoing.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. 'Don't worry about it, I made it all up' acknowledges the problem while completely failing to solve it — Leslie thinks fabricating the alternative makes the question more honest, not less. The logic is beautifully inverted.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I know everything about this town. I'm amazing at my job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Really? What's your area of expertise?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Well, I know that a circle has 360 degrees, and I understand how water flows downhill.

jokes.text: Resident says she's 'not really a fan of parks. Very noisy, barbecue smell all the time.' — a citizen who actively dislikes parks
jokes.setup: Leslie uses the push poll question expecting an easy yes
jokes.punchline: The resident is one of the rare people who genuinely dislikes parks on principle — 'barbecue smell all the time'
jokes.explanation: A nice observational joke built on the premise that Pawnee citizens are perversely contrary. 'Barbecue smell all the time' is specific enough to be funny — not 'I don't like parks' but a very particular sensory grievance. Establishes Pawnee's difficult citizenry.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Lawrence is not a douchebag. He's a good guy who happens to live with his grandmother.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What a douchebag.

jokes.text: Would you change your mind if I told you that nine out of 10 meth users said the same exact thing? / What? / Survey. We surveyed crystal meth users.
jokes.setup: A citizen says he doesn't like parks because of noise and barbecue smells.
jokes.punchline: Leslie deploys the push poll but inverts it — instead of offering a worse alternative, she implies that not liking parks is what meth users believe, apparently backed by a survey she conducted of crystal meth users.
jokes.explanation: A genuine escalation of the push poll joke that goes to a completely unexpected place. 'Survey. We surveyed crystal meth users.' as a deadpan follow-up is brilliant — Leslie has apparently actually surveyed meth users, which raises more questions than it answers. The callback structure is tight, the absurdism is earned, and it's highly quotable. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I play in a band. We're called Mouserat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, we used to be called Scarecrow Boat, but then we changed it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Before that we were The Crackerjacks, and prior to that, Andy and the D-Bags.

jokes.text: You don't care about your kids if you don't support this park! / Excuse me? / It's... What I mean is, kids love parks and you should, too.
jokes.setup: Leslie is getting desperate with a resistant neighbor who mentions his daughter.
jokes.punchline: She shouts that he doesn't care about his kids — a completely inappropriate escalation — before hastily walking it back.
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy where Leslie's passion breaks her composure entirely. What makes it funny rather than just mean is that it accidentally works — his outrage makes him attend to defend himself. The universe rewards Leslie's tactical catastrophe. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I find Kate's aggressive opposition to this park really attractive.

jokes.text: Am I talking to the two sexiest thighs in landscaping? Yes, I am, 'cause I'm talking to Marcy.
jokes.setup: Tom calls a contact at a landscaping company.
jokes.punchline: His opener is an extremely forward compliment directed apparently at a woman named Marcy — delivered with complete confidence as a normal greeting.
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy that relies on Tom's self-regard. The specificity of 'sexiest thighs in landscaping' is funny as a niche compliment. Slightly uncomfortable but character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Reverend Luther Howell founded Pawnee in 1817. He was a man of God, a man of vision, and according to this plaque, he was 'twisted to death' by Native Americans.

jokes.text: Hmm, he said some upsetting things. I can't believe you gave him your home phone number. / Well, I'm a public servant. I need to be accessible.
jokes.setup: They've just left another difficult canvassing interaction.
jokes.punchline: Leslie gave the disturbing man her home phone number, justifying it with complete earnestness as a public servant's duty.
jokes.explanation: The public servant justification is character-perfect for Leslie — she genuinely believes her phone number is a civic resource. The implied horror of what that man might do with it adds a dark edge.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, I've been talking for like twenty minutes, haven't I? Oh my god, I'm doing it again. I'm that person. But you know what? I'm just going to keep going. I'm going to filibuster this conversation. It's a valid political strategy.

jokes.text: Ann! Game changer. You just busted the game wide open. / How? / Andy. We need Andy. He's our symbol. We'll wheel him around the neighborhood to get sympathy. He's a cute FDR.
jokes.setup: Ann mentions Andy's medical bills as a potential sympathy tool.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate leap to wheeling Andy through the neighborhood as a 'cute FDR' is an escalation that's both strategically insane and somehow logical within Leslie's worldview.
jokes.explanation: 'He's a cute FDR' is a brilliantly weird comparison that makes a kind of internal sense: both use wheelchairs, both inspire — but equating an injured local musician to Franklin Roosevelt is absurdist gold. High character integration and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: In the future, Pawnee will have space taxis and we'll communicate through our watches.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, we'll communicate via blinking feelings.

jokes.text: The Sullivan Street Park project. You fast-tracked it, right? / Yeah, absolutely. We have a public forum tomorrow. / Okay. Great. I'll be there. / Great. / Mmm. / 'Hey! You fast-tracked that, right?' [Ron mimicking in private]
jokes.setup: The city manager casually confirms he's coming to the forum, as if it's all fine.
jokes.punchline: Ron, alone, mockingly repeats the city manager's line to himself — revealing his deep private annoyance at being praised for doing something he disagrees with.
jokes.explanation: A subtle but rich moment. Ron's private mockery reveals his full character in a beat: he has to publicly play along with government expansion while privately it fills him with contempt. The talking-head format makes the mimicry funnier because we're his only audience.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I need you to be our youth spokesperson for the parks initiative.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Fine. Parks are... good. You should... use them. I'm very passionate about this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, you have to sound more enthusiastic.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I am enthusiastic. This is my enthusiastic face. Parks are rad. Tubular. Let's get jiggy with it... in the park.

jokes.text: There's a new wind blowing in government and I don't like it.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining his reaction to federal money coming in for parks and community programs.
jokes.punchline: He describes federal investment in public goods as a threatening weather event he has a personal problem with — delivered with complete solemnity.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron Swanson line. 'A new wind blowing in government' is an evocative and ridiculous metaphor applied to something entirely normal. The solemnity with which he says 'and I don't like it' makes it funnier. It also sets up his libertarian worldview efficiently for new viewers.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I just want to say that Leslie Knope has done an amazing job as our parks director. She's made our community better.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: Wait, aren't you the girl who came to my house last week asking me to vote for Leslie?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: ...Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: So you were just canvassing my neighborhood?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: And now you're here saying the same thing?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I... it's a different context.

jokes.text: It's horrifying.
jokes.setup: Ron describes the horror of parks and community programs being funded.
jokes.punchline: One word — 'horrifying' — applied to what is objectively benign civic activity.
jokes.explanation: One word doing maximum work. 'Horrifying' is proportional to a genuine catastrophe; here it's applied to parks. The callback to the previous beat makes it land harder. Economy score is the highest possible — it's a single word.

dialogue.speaker: Resident
dialogue.line: You're just a crazy park lady!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you hear that? They called me a park lady. I'm a park lady!

jokes.text: Do you have, like, a nurse's costume? / Costume? You mean, like, scrubs?
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to use Ann's nurse status as a canvassing prop.
jokes.punchline: He says 'costume' — with all the creepy implications that word carries — and Ann correctly reframes it as 'scrubs,' i.e., actual medical professional clothing.
jokes.explanation: The word 'costume' is doing all the work here — it implies Tom's reference frame is Halloween or something more prurient rather than professional. Ann's deadpan correction is perfect. Short, efficient, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Wait, she actually got me to read The Phantom Tollbooth? From her filibuster?

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ann to put on a 'nurse's costume' — Ann clarifies she means scrubs
jokes.setup: Leslie is preparing Ann to wheel Andy around the neighborhood for sympathy canvassing
jokes.punchline: Leslie asks for a 'nurse's costume,' which Ann correctly identifies as a sexualized Halloween version — then has to specify she means actual medical scrubs
jokes.explanation: A mild misdirection joke. The word 'costume' does all the work — Ann and the audience assume a sexy nurse costume, and then 'You mean like scrubs?' resets it. Functional but not particularly clever or character-specific. Below the episode average in quality.

jokes.text: Why do I want to build this park so bad? Maybe because a pit filled with garbage isn't the best that we can do in America. You know, in Russia, they could pretend that pit was a park, bring their kids down there. 'Hey, Vlad! Look at these rocks! Let's pretend they're potatoes!' 'Nikolai! Do you want to swim in the dirt?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a passionate talking-head confessional about her motivation.
jokes.punchline: Her argument for American exceptionalism is illustrated with a specific imagined Russian scene of children pretending garbage is potatoes and swimming in dirt — delivered with total commitment.
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie Knope monologue. The Cold War logic ('not like Russia') applied to a small Indiana pit is absurdly scaled. 'Do you want to swim in the dirt?' is a genuinely funny line — specific, visual, and delivered with the conviction of a real diplomatic argument. High character integration because only Leslie would frame a neighborhood park in terms of American democratic superiority.

jokes.text: And it is my dream to build a park. That I one day visit with my White House staff on my birthday. And they say, 'President Knope, this park is awesome. Now we understand why you are the first female President of the United States.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been building to an inspiring conclusion about her dream of building the park.
jokes.punchline: The park fantasy escalates: it's not just a park, it's a park she'll visit as President of the United States — specifically the first female President — as a kind of origin story moment.
jokes.explanation: This is a cornerstone Leslie Knope joke that plants her entire character arc in miniature. The absurdity is that this vision is completely sincere — she's not joking about becoming President, she just believes it will happen and is working backwards. 'Now we understand why you are the first female President of the United States' as a line a staffer would deliver is perfectly realized. Maximum character integration — this is the show's thesis statement disguised as a joke. Rewatch value is enormous because the show (spoilers aside) actually honors this aspiration.

jokes.text: Leslie Knope, builder of parks. / How was canvassing? / Canvassing was okay, but I think we're gonna have to postpone the town meeting. / Postpone? / Only for one to 90 days.
jokes.setup: Ron asks how canvassing went.
jokes.punchline: 'Only for one to 90 days' — Leslie's 'small' postponement is actually a three-month window, stated as if that's a trivially minor delay.
jokes.explanation: 'One to 90 days' is the kind of bureaucratic hedge that sounds like a small concession until you realize 90 days is three months. The specificity of the range is what makes it funny — it's not just 'a few months,' it's a formal range that could be almost nothing or almost a season.

jokes.text: I was talking to the city manager, exchanging ideas. Um, there's a mutual respect there. And together, we have decided to fast-track your project.
jokes.setup: Ron is informing Leslie that the project is fast-tracked.
jokes.punchline: Ron describes an exchange with the city manager as a meeting of equals with 'mutual respect' — but we've already seen (Joke 38) that Ron privately mocked the man and resents everything he stands for.
jokes.explanation: Works best on rewatch or for attentive viewers who caught Ron's private mockery. The contrast between his diplomatic language and his actual contempt is rich character comedy. Ron plays the bureaucratic game while despising every rule of it.

jokes.text: I have to cancel this meeting. / Fast-track? / Did my name come up at all? / Oh, this meeting needs to be canceled. / No, it's happening. Look, just do a good job tomorrow. Okay? / Of course. I'll push anything through anything. You know me.
jokes.setup: Ron tells Leslie the project is fast-tracked and the meeting must happen.
jokes.punchline: 'I'll push anything through anything. You know me.' — Leslie's show of confidence is undercut by the gibberish structure of the phrase. 'Push anything through anything' means nothing specific.
jokes.explanation: 'Push anything through anything' is a good verbal stumble that reveals Leslie's nervousness under her performance of confidence. The 'You know me' kicker assumes familiarity that probably doesn't back up the claim.

jokes.text: Tom's pre-meeting schmooze session with contractors — bringing pretzels, saving seats with tape, promoting fence companies, pitching a cement jingle: 'Don's cement / It's the best you can get / Don's'
jokes.setup: Tom is preparing for the town hall meeting by networking with contractors he met while canvassing.
jokes.punchline: He has turned a civic meeting into a networking event complete with snacks, seat reservations, and an improvised company jingle — all for contractors who have nothing to do with the meeting agenda.
jokes.explanation: The cement jingle is the peak of the sequence: completely spontaneous, objectively terrible, and delivered with pride. 'Don's cement / It's the best you can get / Don's' is funny because the third line is just the brand name again, like he ran out of words. Strong character integration — Tom can't help monetizing every situation.

jokes.text: This will be fine, right? It's a park for God's sakes. How much can they hate a park? / A lot of them seemed to hate a park yesterday.
jokes.setup: Ann tries to reassure herself that the meeting will go fine.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, with weary authority, reminds her that empirically, yes, many people hate parks.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the entire canvassing sequence. 'A lot of them seemed to hate a park yesterday' is a perfect deadpan summary of the day's failures. The episodic context makes it land harder.

jokes.text: My mom's here. [pause] No. I can't do that. That's illegal.
jokes.setup: Leslie spots her mother in the audience at the town hall.
jokes.punchline: After a beat of surprise and apparent calculation, she says — to no one — 'No. I can't do that. That's illegal.' The audience never learns what she was considering.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The comedy is entirely in what is NOT said — we never know what illegal thing Leslie considered doing in that moment. The pause is essential; it implies genuine deliberation. 'That's illegal' as a self-restraint note reveals the depth of her desire to impress her mother. Perfectly constructed, highly quotable, and the rewatch value is high because you can project different interpretations onto what she was considering.

jokes.text: Leslie spots her mother in the audience at the town hall — she 'fake invited' her but the mom came anyway
jokes.setup: Earlier, Leslie fake-invited her mother knowing she wouldn't come
jokes.punchline: The mother actually showed up, which is either wonderful or terrible — Leslie's reaction of a silent beat followed by 'No. I can't do that. That's illegal.' implies immediate scheming
jokes.explanation: The callback to the fake invitation pays off with the mother actually showing up. The follow-up line ('No. I can't do that. That's illegal.') is the real joke — Leslie immediately thinks of something involving her mother that she can't do because it's illegal. We never find out what she was contemplating, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: I want my daughter to be successful, which is why I always tell her, 'There's nothing wrong with being a wife and mother.'
jokes.setup: We've been told Leslie's mom is her hero and inspiration.
jokes.punchline: Her version of supporting her daughter's success is to reassure her that marriage and motherhood are valid options — a profound and specific form of non-encouragement.
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating character joke that recontextualizes everything we've seen of Leslie's drive. The joke works on cringe, character, and irony simultaneously. Her mom frames diminished expectations as support. High character integration because it directly explains why Leslie is the way she is.

jokes.text: There are many people that I spoke to who are passionately in support of this idea. None of them were able to make it tonight, unfortunately. But they totally exist. I did not make them up.
jokes.setup: Leslie opens the meeting by citing public support.
jokes.punchline: The reassurance that 'they totally exist. I did not make them up.' is exactly what someone who made them up would say.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured. 'None of them were able to make it tonight' is already a damning statement; 'but they totally exist. I did not make them up.' is the kicker that both defends and convicts. The unprompted denial ('I did not make them up') is classic comedy guilty-conscience logic. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I was warned about by Mark Brendanawicz, our city planner assigned to this project. Uh... So what would he say? [CUT TO:] Here we are.
jokes.setup: Leslie admits she was warned about moving too fast, then appears to wonder what Mark would say.
jokes.punchline: The documentary cuts directly to Mark, as if Leslie summoned him — and he appears with 'Here we are,' an understated acknowledgment of the situation.
jokes.explanation: The edit-as-joke is a mockumentary staple. Works well here because Leslie asking 'What would he say?' followed by immediate cut to Mark arriving is both structurally clean and slightly absurdist. Mark's flat 'Here we are' is a good landing.

jokes.text: Mark Brendanawicz knows the answer to every question. He's amazing and congratulations for hearing him speak. / Hi there. Leslie might have oversold me a little bit. / Certainly did not. He's the man. He's capable of anything.
jokes.setup: Leslie introduces Mark to the audience.
jokes.punchline: Her introduction escalates into 'congratulations for hearing him speak' — as if his speaking is a prize citizens have won. Mark's modest correction ('oversold me a little bit') is immediately rejected.
jokes.explanation: 'Congratulations for hearing him speak' is a genuinely funny construction — it positions hearing a city planner describe a rectangular lot as a privilege. Leslie's double-down of 'He's capable of anything' after his gentle correction is a good escalation.

jokes.text: Lot 48 is... It's a rectangular lot. It's got excellent drainage. And it's on the corner of Sullivan and Collins. Any questions?
jokes.setup: Leslie has described Mark as knowing 'the answer to every question' and being 'capable of anything.'
jokes.punchline: His entire presentation consists of three sentences: it's rectangular, it drains well, and here's where it is. The underdelivery after the enormous buildup is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback payoff. Leslie has built up enormous expectations, and Mark delivers the most minimal possible presentation. 'It's got excellent drainage' as a highlight is particularly good. The structure is tight: setup (Leslie's wild praise) → payoff (Mark's three sentences). Economy is near-perfect. Gets a genuinely big laugh from the contrast alone.

jokes.text: Uh, yeah. I don't care about any of that. He's the guy that plays music all night in his garage. It's driving me nuts. / Lawrence lives with his grandma.
jokes.setup: A citizen stands up with what appears to be a comment about Andy as the victim who fell in the pit.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't care about the pit — he's there to complain about Andy's band. Leslie's aside 'Lawrence lives with his grandma' is delivered as a counterattack.
jokes.explanation: The subversion of the 'sympathetic citizen' moment into a neighbor grievance is well-executed. 'Lawrence lives with his grandma' as Leslie's weapon of choice is funny because she's weaponizing an irrelevant life detail. The town hall devolving into personal squabbles is great structural comedy.

jokes.text: Which is pretty awesome. He takes care of her, I guess. But whatever, he's a douchebag. It's loud, it's abusive, and it's waking up my birds.
jokes.setup: Lawrence has been called out for living with his grandma.
jokes.punchline: He concedes the grandma point — 'which is pretty awesome, he takes care of her, I guess' — before pivoting back to his grievance with a list that climaxes in 'waking up my birds.'
jokes.explanation: The brief self-aware concession before the pivot is funny — he's not totally unreasonable. 'Waking up my birds' as the final complaint is the right amount of bathos after 'loud' and 'abusive.'

jokes.text: Lawrence complains about Andy's music: 'it wakes them up.' Andy: 'You have birds, now?' Lawrence: 'Yeah, I have birds. I have nice, pretty, expensive birds.'
jokes.setup: Lawrence is complaining about Andy's music at a public town hall about a park
jokes.punchline: The complaint is about waking up birds — then the escalation to 'nice, pretty, expensive birds' as a justification takes the complaint in an unexpectedly specific direction
jokes.explanation: 'Nice, pretty, expensive birds' is a funny escalation — each adjective adds a different dimension (aesthetic, financial, personal investment) to the bird grievance. The specificity works. Also, the entire complaint being about birds rather than, say, sleep, is delightfully petty.

jokes.text: And actually, if anyone here plays bass, we need a bassist.
jokes.setup: Andy is at a town hall meeting to provide sympathy support for a park proposal.
jokes.punchline: He uses the public forum as an opportunity to recruit a bassist for his band.
jokes.explanation: Andy derailing a civic meeting to recruit musicians is perfectly in character and escalates organically from the previous lines. The complete lack of self-awareness about context is Andy's defining trait, and it's executed with maximum economy here. A strong candidate for standout moment.

jokes.text: Uh. It is not going well at all. Mmm-hmm. It's going very poorly. Okay? Mmm-hmm. Like, you're crashing and burning. Democracy's happening. People are talking. I mean, at least they aren't apathetic, right?
jokes.setup: Mark delivers a blunt assessment of the disaster.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reframes a total catastrophe as 'democracy happening' and civic engagement — finding the positive spin on the worst possible outcome.
jokes.explanation: Great character pair moment. Mark's escalating frankness ('not going well' → 'very poorly' → 'crashing and burning') builds perfectly for Leslie's pivot to 'Democracy's happening.' Her optimism reframe is both sincere and delusional, which is her essential comedy engine.

jokes.text: Andy announces his band is called 'Just the Tip' at a public town hall
jokes.setup: Andy is defending himself against Lawrence's noise complaint
jokes.punchline: 'I'm in a band. It's called Just the Tip.' — the band name's double entendre lands in a formal civic setting
jokes.explanation: The double entendre band name dropped at a city council meeting is perfectly Andy — he has no idea (or doesn't care) about the context. 'Guilty as charged' before the name reveal is a good escalation beat. The joke is in the name's inappropriateness for the setting.

jokes.text: I'm oddly attracted to Kate Spivack.
jokes.setup: Mark and Leslie are discussing how to save the meeting. Kate Spivack is the woman who organized opposition to the park.
jokes.punchline: Mark volunteers this completely unprompted personal information as if it's relevant to the damage-control strategy.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best short jokes. The timing is perfect — it comes in the middle of a crisis strategy conversation as if it's a tactical point. 'Oddly' is the right qualifier, acknowledging his own inconvenient attraction. High economy (six words), high surprise, strong character note for Mark as someone not fully invested in the project.

jokes.text: Mark's confessional: 'I'm oddly attracted to Kate Spivack.'
jokes.setup: The meeting has just been chaotic; Kate Spivack has been the most hostile voice
jokes.punchline: Mark confesses to finding the most aggressive opponent in the room attractive
jokes.explanation: Five words, complete character beat. 'Oddly attracted to Kate Spivack' is economical and specific — the word 'oddly' is doing most of the work, acknowledging that this is the wrong response to hostility. It's Mark's version of self-awareness: he knows this is irrational and says so. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: The City of Pawnee was incorporated in 1817, when a young man by the name of Reverend Luther Howell came from Terre Haute on an ox. He planted his flag in the ground and was met soon after by an angry tribe of Wamapoke Indians, who, when seeing the whiteness of his skin, twisted him to death.
jokes.setup: Leslie decides to 'give a little history of Pawnee' to buy time at the meeting.
jokes.punchline: Pawnee's founding story involves the founder being 'twisted to death' — a dark, specific, and deeply unheroic founding mythology delivered as if it's an inspiring origin story.
jokes.explanation: 'Twisted him to death' is a wonderfully specific and absurd form of violence. The joke works because Leslie tells this story with civic pride, as if being twisted to death by indigenous people who were defending their land is a charming founding anecdote. It also seeds the Parks universe's dark history of Pawnee's relationship with the Wamapoke, which becomes a recurring theme.

jokes.text: My, God. She's filibustering her own meeting. / Filibuster! Boom! They can't touch you if you talk forever.
jokes.setup: Mark realizes what Leslie is doing with the history lecture.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately celebrates the tactic with 'Filibuster! Boom!' — as if it's a clever play rather than a desperate stall by someone reading a children's book at a civic meeting.
jokes.explanation: Tom's enthusiasm for Leslie's desperate tactic is well-calibrated. 'They can't touch you if you talk forever' is both true as a procedural point and absurd as a governing philosophy. Good character pair joke.

jokes.text: The future of Pawnee will involve us flying around in space taxis, where we will communicate on watches, and blink our feelings to each other, rather than use words.
jokes.setup: Leslie is filibustering by predicting Pawnee's future.
jokes.punchline: Her vision of the future involves 'blinking feelings' at each other instead of using words — a specific and completely novel form of non-verbal communication that she says with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: 'Blink our feelings to each other' is a genuinely original absurdist image. It's specific enough to be funny on its own merits. The space taxis and watch communication are also good period-appropriate future-speak jokes.

jokes.text: And now, I'd like to take a magical journey through a little something I like to call The Phantom Tollbooth, by Norton Juster.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been filibustering with history and future-casting.
jokes.punchline: Her next stall tactic is to read a children's novel aloud at a civic meeting — complete with 'magical journey' framing as if this is a legitimate agenda item.
jokes.explanation: The specific title is important — The Phantom Tollbooth is a real, beloved children's book, which makes the choice funnier than a made-up one. 'A magical journey through a little something I like to call' is a great absurdist framing. The confidence is total.

jokes.text: That girl over there with the long brown hair and the yellow top. Could you tell us how you feel about this park? / Hi. Uh, I'm a youth in the community and I think a new park is a great idea. And I fully support it, as would the rest of the youth in the community.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been told to find positive voices; she calls on April, her plant in the audience.
jokes.punchline: April delivers the most robotically scripted possible testimonial — 'I'm a youth in the community' — and the contrast between her deadpan delivery and the wooden script makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm a youth in the community' is perfectly terrible — no actual young person would describe themselves this way. April's deadpan makes it land harder. Good setup/payoff structure using the plant reveal.

jokes.text: Hey! I recognize her. That kid came to my door yesterday. Oh, my God! Okay, they have planted people in this audience.
jokes.setup: April has delivered her scripted testimonial.
jokes.punchline: A citizen immediately recognizes April from canvassing, blowing the plant's cover — escalating the meeting disaster to a new level.
jokes.explanation: A great callback that makes the canvassing sequence retroactively funnier. Leslie's elaborate operation has backfired because Pawnee is small enough that people recognize each other. The escalation of the meeting failure is well-paced.

jokes.text: A couple of weeks ago, I was yelling at Leslie at a public forum. God, I hope I wasn't as obnoxious as those people. I wasn't, right?
jokes.setup: Ann watches the chaotic meeting and reflects on the opposition's behavior.
jokes.punchline: She realizes she was recently on the other side of this — yelling at Leslie at a public forum — and immediately seeks reassurance that she was less bad, without any external confirmation available.
jokes.explanation: A great meta-moment that rewards viewers who've seen the pilot. Ann's self-awareness is partial — she recognizes the parallel but can't quite admit she was probably just as bad. The unanswered 'I wasn't, right?' hanging in the air is the real joke. Good character development disguised as a gag.

jokes.text: At 5:00 in the morning, every morning, beep, beep, beep! I don't want to hear that. Now, how long is this project gonna take? That's what I want to know. That's what's important to me. Because I need my sleep.
jokes.setup: Citizens are lining up to speak about the park.
jokes.punchline: The citizen's concern about the project is that construction will wake her up — her complaint is entirely self-centered and has nothing to do with the park's merits.
jokes.explanation: Observational joke about public meetings — the disconnect between civic process and petty personal concerns. Functionally funny but not particularly surprising or character-specific.

jokes.text: Thank you, ma'am. That concludes our meeting. / What about the vote? / We're out of time. It's 9:00. But we will have many public forums in the future, and we hope to see you all there.
jokes.setup: After a citizen's complaint, Leslie abruptly ends the meeting.
jokes.punchline: She uses the ending time as cover to avoid the vote that would defeat her, framing her escape as proper process with 'we hope to see you all there.'
jokes.explanation: The meeting escape is telegraphed by Mark's earlier advice ('avoid a vote'), so the payoff is satisfying. 'We hope to see you all there' for a future meeting the audience just tried to destroy is the right absurdist button.

jokes.text: God, I loved it! I loved every minute of it. / Hey, park lady. / Yeah? / You suck.
jokes.setup: Leslie is reflecting warmly on the meeting, finding genuine joy in the democratic process despite its chaos.
jokes.punchline: A citizen walks past and says simply 'You suck.' Leslie's response is to receive it as neutral feedback.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing and structure. The setup is Leslie at her most optimistic and self-congratulatory; the punchline is two words of brutal democratic feedback. The economy is almost perfect. What elevates it is the callback beat that follows.

jokes.text: Hear that? He called me 'park lady.'
jokes.setup: A citizen just told Leslie she sucks.
jokes.punchline: Leslie completely filters out the insult and focuses on the title 'park lady' as an honor — a designation that confirms her identity and mission.
jokes.explanation: The episode's peak joke and a defining character moment. 'Hear that? He called me park lady.' is extraordinary because it inverts the entire meaning of the insult through Leslie's filter. She has taken 'you suck' and extracted only the title as validation. It's funny, it's moving, it's character-perfect, and it's quotable. Maximum character integration — this line couldn't be said by anyone else on any other show. The pivot from joke to character revelation to series thesis statement in four words is genuinely excellent writing.

jokes.text: You know, normally, I don't agree with Leslie about anything, but this book is awesome.
jokes.setup: Leslie had been reading The Phantom Tollbooth at the town hall meeting as a stall tactic.
jokes.punchline: Ron — who opposes everything Leslie stands for — has apparently read The Phantom Tollbooth and genuinely loves it. The final image is Ron Swanson endorsing a children's book.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful closing joke that works on multiple levels: it's a callback to the stall-tactic reading, it reveals a warm dimension of Ron beneath his libertarian armor, and it ends the episode on an unexpected note of agreement. 'Normally, I don't agree with Leslie about anything' states the premise; the pivot to a children's book is the absurdist twist. High character integration because Ron's private literary life (vs. his public persona) is the joke. A great episode button.

tmdb_overview: Leslie decides that she and her committee need to go door-to-door to gain support for the park project as well as support for an upcoming town hall meeting, but their mission does not go as planned. Meanwhile, Tom wanders away from the canvassing group and uses his own creative recruitment tactics.
insight: Leslie's earnest incompetence drives 38 jokes in a scrappy early pilot.
